# The Old Night

On January 17, 1994, at half past four in the morning, an earthquake knocked out power across Los Angeles. The shaking woke people up, but so did the sky. Thousands of startled residents looked out their windows and saw something they couldn't account for: a vast silvery cloud hanging above the darkened city. Calls poured into emergency services and into the Griffith Observatory, where confused callers demanded to know what the strange thing was. The strange thing was the Milky Way. The earthquake had, in one stroke, switched off the lights over a metropolis of millions, and in the sudden dark the galaxy appeared — the galaxy that had arched over every human night for two hundred thousand years, and which vanished again a few days later when the power grid was patched back together.

What those callers saw, briefly and by accident, is something nearly all of us now live our whole lives without: night. Not the absence of daylight, not the hours when we stay indoors with the lamps on, but the night itself — real darkness, the oldest darkness, the kind our ancestors lived inside for half of every day of their lives. It is now, arguably, one of the rarest experiences on Earth. You can still find unlogged forest and untracked desert, but genuine darkness — darkness deep enough to swallow a city — survives only in scattered reserves, islands of the old night in an ocean of new light.

The old night was not a dimmer version of the day. It was a different country, with its own laws, its own dangers, and its own graces. Its border was called curfew — a word that comes from the French *couvre-feu*, "cover the fire," the hour when hearths were banked and cities pulled their gates shut. English law once recognized a class of offender called the nightwalker, a person abroad in the dark without good cause. In London you could hire a link-boy — a child with a flaming torch — to see you home, the way you might hail a taxi today. To keep watch was to hold a vigil, from the Latin for wakefulness; the word has drifted, but it remembers. Even moonlight was infrastructure. The full moon nearest the autumn equinox was the harvest moon, and it mattered because it rose soon after sunset for several nights running, stretching the workday out into the fields. In Ireland, well into the nineteenth century, the mail coaches ran to lunar timetables: the roads were so rough and the dark so complete that the post could travel at speed only under a full moon.

And darkness changed what the senses did. With sight extinguished, hearing bloomed. People heard their world: footsteps on frost, owls exchanging calls, an animal moving through brush, a stream running somewhere out in the black. The failure of the eyes made room for the imagination, and the imagination is a prolific colonist. The old night was haunted — of course it was haunted. Every culture settled the darkness with ghosts, revenants, demons, and things that waited just past the reach of the firelight. The word *nightmare* preserves a piece of this settlement: the mare was a spirit that crept in at night and sat on sleepers' chests. It seems likely people were describing, in folklore, the real and terrifying experience of sleep paralysis — the mind waking into a body still pinned by dreams — but the deeper point is that darkness was populated, because in the dark the mind supplies whatever the eyes cannot confirm. Ghost stories and campfires belong to the same technology. They were how the old dark was furnished.

One of the strangest things we have learned about that world is that our ancestors slept differently in it. For most of the twentieth century, historians assumed people had always slept as we do, in one consolidated lump. Then the historian Roger Ekirch, combing through diaries, court records, medical texts, letters, and literature from the pre-industrial West, kept running into a phrase that shouldn't have existed: *first sleep*. There it was, over and over — first sleep, and its counterpart, second sleep — in prayers and novels and court depositions, in French (*premier somme*), Italian (*primo sonno*), German (*erster Schlaf*). Anthropologists working in West Africa recorded the Tiv of Nigeria using first sleep and second sleep as ordinary markers of time, the way we say *noon* or *midnight*.

The pattern the documents describe is this: people went to bed a couple of hours after dark, slept deeply for three or four hours, and then woke. Not woke in distress — woke naturally, into an interval of quiet wakefulness that lasted an hour or more, and then drifted back into a second sleep until dawn. Ekirch found that the waking interval had a life of its own. People prayed; the old night prayers were said specifically then. They tended the embers. They talked with family or neighbors. They pondered their dreams, which surfaced easily in the stillness — one reason dreams loom so much larger in pre-modern culture than in ours. And they had sex: early-modern advice literature, of all things, recommended the interval after first sleep as the best time for conception, the body rested and the mind unhurried. The French even had a word, *dorveille*, for the hovering state between sleeping and waking — a word that exists because millions of people passed through that state every night of their lives and needed a name for it.

The clincher came from a laboratory. In the 1990s, the sleep researcher Thomas Wehr ran an experiment in which volunteers spent a month with fourteen hours of darkness — roughly the light regime of a winter night before electricity. At first the subjects slept the standard modern way, about eight hours straight. But as the weeks passed, their sleep began to reorganize. It split. Unprompted, they settled into the old pattern: a solid block of sleep, then an hour or two of calm wakefulness — during which their blood showed elevated prolactin, a hormone associated with quiet, placid states — then a second block of sleep. Given darkness enough, the two-shift night reappeared, as though it had been waiting in the biology all along.

Which suggests something quietly radical about a very common experience. Waking at two or three in the morning and lying awake, anxious,

# The Old Night

On January 17, 1994, at half past four in the morning, an earthquake knocked out power across Los Angeles. The shaking woke people up, but so did the sky. Thousands of startled Angelenos looked out their windows and saw something they couldn't account for: a vast silvery cloud hanging over the darkened city. Calls poured into emergency services and into the Griffith Observatory, where confused residents demanded to know what the strange thing was. The strange thing was the Milky Way. The earthquake, in one stroke, had switched off the lights over a city of ten million, and in the sudden dark the galaxy appeared — the galaxy that had arched over every human night for two hundred thousand years, and which vanished again a few hours later when the power grid was patched back together.

What those callers saw, briefly and by accident, is something that nearly all of us now live our whole lives without: night. Not the absence of daylight, not the hours when we stay indoors with the lamps on, but the night itself — real darkness, the oldest darkness, the kind our ancestors lived inside for half of every day of their lives. It is now, arguably, one of the rarest experiences on Earth. There are places in the world where you can still find unlogged forest and untrampled tundra, but genuine darkness — darkness that swallows cities — has retreated to a few scattered reserves, islands of the old night in an ocean of new light.

The old night was not a dimmer version of the day. It was a different country, with its own laws, its own dangers, and its own graces. Its border was called curfew — a word that comes from the French couvre-feu, "cover the fire," the hour when hearths were banked and cities pulled their gates shut. English law once recognized a class of offender called the nightwalker, a person abroad in the dark without cause. To keep watch was to hold a vigil, from the Latin for wakefulness — the word has drifted, but it remembers. Even moonlight was infrastructure. The full moon nearest the autumn equinox was the harvest moon, and it mattered so much because it rose near sunset for several nights in a row, extending the workday into the field. In Ireland, well into the nineteenth century, the mail coaches ran to lunar timetables: the roads were so bad, and the dark so complete, that the post traveled at speed only under a full moon.

And darkness changed what the senses did. With sight extinguished, hearing bloomed. People heard their world at night: footsteps on frost, owls, the small talk of animals, a stream miles off. Sight's failure made room for imagination, and imagination is a prolific colonist. The old night was haunted — of course it was haunted. Every culture settled the darkness with ghosts, revenants, demons, and things that waited just past the reach of the firelight. The word nightmare preserves a piece of this settlement: the mare was a spirit that crept in at night and sat on sleepers' chests. It seems likely that people were describing, with their folklore, the real and terrifying experience of sleep paralysis — the mind waking into a body still pinned in dreams — but the point is that darkness was populated, because in the dark the mind supplied whatever the eyes could not confirm.

[Then Ekirch]

One of the strangest things we've learned about the old night is that our ancestors slept differently in it. For most of the twentieth century, historians assumed that people have always slept as we do, in one consolidated lump. Then the historian Roger Ekirch, combing through diaries, court records, medical texts, letters, and literature from the pre-industrial West, kept running into a phrase that shouldn't have existed: first sleep. There it was, over and over — first sleep, and its counterpart, second sleep — in fifteenth-century prayers and eighteenth-century novels, in French (premier somme), Italian (primo sonno), German (erster Schlaf). Anthropologists working among the Tiv of Nigeria recorded that same culture using first sleep and second sleep as ordinary markers of time, the way we say noon or midnight.

The pattern the documents describe is this: people went to bed a couple of hours after dark, slept deeply for three or four hours, and then woke. Not woke in distress — woke naturally, into an interval of quiet wakefulness that lasted an hour or more, and then drifted back into a second sleep until dawn. Ekirch found that the waking interval had a life of its own. People prayed — the old night prayers were said specifically there. They tended the embers. They talked. They pondered their dreams, which were vivid and easily recalled in the stillness, which is one reason dreams loom so much larger in pre-modern culture than in ours. And they had sex: early-modern advice literature, of all things, recommended the interval after first sleep as the best time for conception, the body rested and the mind at ease. The French even had a word, dorveille, for that hovering state between sleep and waking — a word that exists because millions of people passed through the state every night and needed a name for it.

The clincher came from a laboratory. In the 1990s, the sleep researcher Thomas Wehr ran an experiment in which volunteers spent a month with fourteen hours of darkness — mimicking, roughly, the light conditions of a winter night before electricity. At first the subjects simply slept the standard human way, about eight hours straight. But as the weeks passed, their sleep began to reorganize. It split. They settled, unprompted, into the old pattern: a solid block of sleep, then an hour or two of calm wakefulness — during which their blood showed elevated prolactin, a hormone associated with quiet, contented states — then another block of sleep. Given darkness enough, the two-shift night reappeared, as if it had been waiting in the biology all along.

Which suggests something quietly radical about a very common experience. Waking at two or three in the morning and lying awake, anxious, is usually treated as a malfunction — insomnia, something wrong. But it may in many cases be a fossil: the old pattern stirring in a body built for it, surfacing into a world that no longer recognizes the waking hour, has no place for it, and offers nothing but the mute red glare of an alarm clock. The anxiety may not be the cause of the wakefulness so much as its context. The hour of quiet was once a room of the house. We removed the room and kept the hour.

[Light economics]

What unmade that world was, above all, light. And light, for almost all of human history, was dear — a luxury the way spices were luxuries. The poor burned rushlights: reeds peeled and dipped in kitchen fat, giving a flame worth less than a candle and smelling like a fryer. Tallow candles were better and stank; beeswax candles were lovely and expensive; whale oil, later, burned bright and clean, and the desire for it sent fleets to the ends of the oceans. An hour of decent light could cost a laborer a meaningful chunk of a day's wages. When your light is that expensive, you don't spend it reading. You spend it sparingly, briefly, and you sleep in the dark, because the dark is free.

Then, in a single century, the price collapsed. In 1807, gaslight made its public debut on Pall Mall in London, and the streets themselves began to glow. In 1879 Edison's team produced a practical incandescent bulb; in 1882 his Pearl Street Station began delivering electricity to a section of Lower Manhattan, and the modern night began to die. The death took a hundred years, and it was total. Cities that had once sealed themselves behind gates against the dark now ran all night. Midnight stopped being a border and became a social hour. Night work, night shifts, night menus. The night did not get smaller — it got absorbed. It became, for most of the developed world, day with the dimmer turned down.

[Stars]

The cost of the transaction was posted on the ceiling, and most of us have never read the bill. In 2016, an international team produced the first comprehensive atlas of artificial night sky brightness and found that more than 80 percent of humanity lives under light-polluted skies — that the Milky Way is hidden from more than a third of all people, from 60 percent of Europeans, from 80 percent of North Americans. Meanwhile the lights keep advancing: satellite measurements from recent years show the artificially lit surface of the planet growing in area and brightness by roughly two percent annually. A hundred generations ago the Milky Way was the single most conspicuous object in the human night. Today most people in wealthy countries will see it only if they travel to see it, the way one travels to a glacier.

What is being lost is not just a pretty view. Every culture that ever looked up wove meaning out of that band of light. The Greeks saw spilled milk from Hera's breast; the Chinese saw a river of stars dividing two lovers, the Weaver Girl and the Herd Boy, who meet one night a year on a bridge of magpies. The !Kung of the Kalahari called the Milky Way the Backbone of Night, which is maybe the best name anyone has given it. Polynesian navigators read the night sky the way you or I read a road sign, and found islands across thousands of miles of open ocean. The sky was humanity's calendar, compass, scripture, and clock. Kant wrote of the starry heavens above as one of the two things that filled him with awe, and he had a poor view by the standards of his century — his city, Königsberg, had gaslight in nothing; his Milky Way was the real thing. Awe of that kind was once the default setting of the human night. Now it is a destination.

[Body]

There is also this: darkness turns out to be a biological need. In the 1990s and early 2000s, researchers worked out that a subset of cells in the eye respond to light not for vision at all but to tell the brain what time it is — and that these cells are most sensitive to blue wavelengths, the color of sky. Light in those wavelengths, arriving at night, suppresses melatonin, the hormone the pineal gland releases in darkness to set the body's long night in motion. This is why the tablet you scroll at midnight, with its little blue sun, whispers to your brainstem that it is noon. Chronic disruption of these rhythms is linked to poor sleep, mood disorders, metabolic trouble; the World Health Organization's cancer agency has classified shift work that disrupts circadian rhythms as a probable human carcinogen. Whatever else the old dark was, it was a nutrient. We have been on a kind of diet for a century, and the deficiency is showing.

[Dark-sky movement]

The good news is that the loss is, to a degree almost unique among environmental wounds, reversible. Flip the switch back and the stars return — instantly, completely, no cleanup required. Since 1988, the International Dark-Sky Association has certified dark-sky places around the world, beginning with Natural Bridges National Monument in Utah in 2007. Cities are learning to shield their fixtures and warm their bulbs so light falls on streets rather than up at the sky. And people who make the trip to a truly dark place often report that the experience is stranger and more moving than they expected. Park rangers tell of visitors going silent under the first truly dark sky they've ever seen; some weep. Under the very best skies — moonless, dry, at altitude — the Milky Way is not a smudge but a structure, the bright rift and the Great Rift within it, and some observers swear it is bright enough to cast a faint shadow on pale ground. Starlight, casting shadows. That used to be the ordinary furniture of the night.

[Close]

It's worth trying to say what darkness is, since we've spent a century acting as if it were nothing — a mere absence, a defect, the universe's way of failing to be lit. But darkness is older than light in our story. We are day creatures who came out of the dark; every one of our ancestors, for four billion years, lived nested in it, and the fire beside which our lineage gathered for the last million years has always been a small island ringed by an enormous, breathing continent. Even cosmically the point holds: all the visible stars, all the galaxies, amount to a rounding error in a universe that is better than 95 percent dark.

Enclosing the commons of the night took about a century, and it was done not out of malice but out of the ordinary human wish to see and be safe. But enclosure can be undone in patches, and unlike most restorations, this one is instant. So: go find it. A desert, a mountainside, a national park, any place the nearest city is a faint dome on the horizon rather than a sky. Go on a moonless night. Wait half an hour while your eyes quietly rebuild their ancient instrument. Then look up. The band of light overhead is the galaxy we live inside, seen edge-on from within — a hundred billion suns behind a hundred billion veils — and it is beautiful, and it was there above every human who ever lived until the last few generations, and it will be there tonight, whether or not anyone is awake to see it.

# The Old Night

On January 17, 1994, at half past four in the morning, an earthquake knocked out power across Los Angeles. The shaking woke people up, but so did the sky. Thousands of startled Angelenos looked out their windows and saw something they couldn't account for: a vast silvery cloud hanging over the darkened city. Calls poured into emergency services and into the Griffith Observatory, where confused residents demanded to know what the strange thing was. The strange thing was the Milky Way. The earthquake, in one stroke, had switched off the lights over a city of ten million, and in the sudden dark the galaxy appeared — the galaxy that had arched over every human night for two hundred thousand years, and which vanished again a few hours later when the power grid was patched back together.

What those callers saw, briefly and by accident, is something that nearly all of us now live our whole lives without: night. Not the absence of daylight, not the hours when we stay indoors with the lamps on, but the night itself — real darkness, the oldest darkness, the kind our ancestors lived inside for half of every day of their lives. It is now, arguably, one of the rarest experiences on Earth. There are places in the world where you can still find unlogged forest and untrampled tundra, but genuine darkness — darkness that swallows cities — has retreated to a few scattered reserves, islands of the old night in an ocean of new light.

The old night was not a dimmer version of the day. It was a different country, with its own laws, its own dangers, and its own graces. Its border was called curfew — a word that comes from the French couvre-feu, "cover the fire," the hour when hearths were banked and cities pulled their gates shut. English law once recognized a class of offender called the nightwalker, a person abroad in the dark without cause. To keep watch was to hold a vigil, from the Latin for wakefulness — the word has drifted, but it remembers. Even moonlight was infrastructure. The full moon nearest the autumn equinox was the harvest moon, and it mattered so much because it rose near sunset for several nights in a row, extending the workday into the field. In Ireland, well into the nineteenth century, the mail coaches ran to lunar timetables: the roads were so bad, and the dark so complete, that the post traveled at speed only under a full moon.

And darkness changed what the senses did. With sight extinguished, hearing bloomed. People heard their world at night: footsteps on frost, owls, the small talk of animals, a stream miles off. Sight's failure made room for imagination, and imagination is a prolific colonist. The old night was haunted — of course it was haunted. Every culture settled the darkness with ghosts, revenants, demons, and things that waited just past the reach of the firelight. The word nightmare preserves a piece of this settlement: the mare was a spirit that crept in at night and sat on sleepers' chests. It seems likely that people were describing, with their folklore, the real and terrifying experience of sleep paralysis — the mind waking into a body still pinned in dreams — but the point is that darkness was populated, because in the dark the mind supplied whatever the eyes could not confirm.

[Then Ekirch]

One of the strangest things we've learned about the old night is that our ancestors slept differently in it. For most of the twentieth century, historians assumed that people have always slept as we do, in one consolidated lump. Then the historian Roger Ekirch, combing through diaries, court records, medical texts, letters, and literature from the pre-industrial West, kept running into a phrase that shouldn't have existed: first sleep. There it was, over and over — first sleep, and its counterpart, second sleep — in fifteenth-century prayers and eighteenth-century novels, in French (premier somme), Italian (primo sonno), German (erster Schlaf). Anthropologists working among the Tiv of Nigeria recorded that same culture using first sleep and second sleep as ordinary markers of time, the way we say noon or midnight.

The pattern the documents describe is this: people went to bed a couple of hours after dark, slept deeply for three or four hours, and then woke. Not woke in distress — woke naturally, into an interval of quiet wakefulness that lasted an hour or more, and then drifted back into a second sleep until dawn. Ekirch found that the waking interval had a life of its own. People prayed — the old night prayers were said specifically there. They tended the embers. They talked. They pondered their dreams, which were vivid and easily recalled in the stillness, which is one reason dreams loom so much larger in pre-modern culture than in ours. And they had sex: early-modern advice literature, of all things, recommended the interval after first sleep as the best time for conception, the body rested and the mind at ease. The French even had a word, dorveille, for that hovering state between sleep and waking — a word that exists because millions of people passed through the state every night and needed a name for it.

The clincher came from a laboratory. In the 1990s, the sleep researcher Thomas Wehr ran an experiment in which volunteers spent a month with fourteen hours of darkness — mimicking, roughly, the light conditions of a winter night before electricity. At first the subjects simply slept the standard human way, about eight hours straight. But as the weeks passed, their sleep began to reorganize. It split. They settled, unprompted, into the old pattern: a solid block of sleep, then an hour or two of calm wakefulness — during which their blood showed elevated prolactin, a hormone associated with quiet, contented states — then another block of sleep. Given darkness enough, the two-shift night reappeared, as if it had been waiting in the biology all along.

Which suggests something quietly radical about a very common experience. Waking at two or three in the morning and lying awake, anxious, is usually treated as a malfunction — insomnia, something wrong. But it may in many cases be a fossil: the old pattern stirring in a body built for it, surfacing into a world that no longer recognizes the waking hour, has no place for it, and offers nothing but the mute red glare of an alarm clock. The anxiety may not be the cause of the wakefulness so much as its context. The hour of quiet was once a room of the house. We removed the room and kept the hour.

[Light economics]

What unmade that world was, above all, light. And light, for almost all of human history, was dear — a luxury the way spices were luxuries. The poor burned rushlights: reeds peeled and dipped in kitchen fat, giving a flame worth less than a candle and smelling like a fryer. Tallow candles were better and stank; beeswax candles were lovely and expensive; whale oil, later, burned bright and clean, and the desire for it sent fleets to the ends of the oceans. An hour of decent light could cost a laborer a meaningful chunk of a day's wages. When your light is that expensive, you don't spend it reading. You spend it sparingly, briefly, and you sleep in the dark, because the dark is free.

Then, in a single century, the price collapsed. In 1807, gaslight made its public debut on Pall Mall in London, and the streets themselves began to glow. In 1879 Edison's team produced a practical incandescent bulb; in 1882 his Pearl Street Station began delivering electricity to a section of Lower Manhattan, and the modern night began to die. The death took a hundred years, and it was total. Cities that had once sealed themselves behind gates against the dark now ran all night. Midnight stopped being a border and became a social hour. Night work, night shifts, night menus. The night did not get smaller — it got absorbed. It became, for most of the developed world, day with the dimmer turned down.

[Stars]

The cost of the transaction was posted on the ceiling, and most of us have never read the bill. In 2016, an international team produced the first comprehensive atlas of artificial night sky brightness and found that more than 80 percent of humanity lives under light-polluted skies — that the Milky Way is hidden from more than a third of all people, from 60 percent of Europeans, from 80 percent of North Americans. Meanwhile the lights keep advancing: satellite measurements from recent years show the artificially lit surface of the planet growing in area and brightness by roughly two percent annually. A hundred generations ago the Milky Way was the single most conspicuous object in the human night. Today most people in wealthy countries will see it only if they travel to see it, the way one travels to a glacier.

What is being lost is not just a pretty view. Every culture that ever looked up wove meaning out of that band of light. The Greeks saw spilled milk from Hera's breast; the Chinese saw a river of stars dividing two lovers, the Weaver Girl and the Herd Boy, who meet one night a year on a bridge of magpies. The !Kung of the Kalahari called the Milky Way the Backbone of Night, which is maybe the best name anyone has given it. Polynesian navigators read the night sky the way you or I read a road sign, and found islands across thousands of miles of open ocean. The sky was humanity's calendar, compass, scripture, and clock. Kant wrote of the starry heavens above as one of the two things that filled him with awe, and he had a poor view by the standards of his century — his city, Königsberg, had gaslight in nothing; his Milky Way was the real thing. Awe of that kind was once the default setting of the human night. Now it is a destination.

[Body]

There is also this: darkness turns out to be a biological need. In the 1990s and early 2000s, researchers worked out that a subset of cells in the eye respond to light not for vision at all but to tell the brain what time it is — and that these cells are most sensitive to blue wavelengths, the color of sky. Light in those wavelengths, arriving at night, suppresses melatonin, the hormone the pineal gland releases in darkness to set the body's long night in motion. This is why the tablet you scroll at midnight, with its little blue sun, whispers to your brainstem that it is noon. Chronic disruption of these rhythms is linked to poor sleep, mood disorders, metabolic trouble; the World Health Organization's cancer agency has classified shift work that disrupts circadian rhythms as a probable human carcinogen. Whatever else the old dark was, it was a nutrient. We have been on a kind of diet for a century, and the deficiency is showing.

[Dark-sky movement]

The good news is that the loss is, to a degree almost unique among environmental wounds, reversible. Flip the switch back and the stars return — instantly, completely, no cleanup required. Since 1988, the International Dark-Sky Association has certified dark-sky places around the world, beginning with Natural Bridges National Monument in Utah in 2007. Cities are learning to shield their fixtures and warm their bulbs so light falls on streets rather than up at the sky. And people who make the trip to a truly dark place often report that the experience is stranger and more moving than they expected. Park rangers tell of visitors going silent under the first truly dark sky they've ever seen; some weep. Under the very best skies — moonless, dry, at altitude — the Milky Way is not a smudge but a structure, the bright rift and the Great Rift within it, and some observers swear it is bright enough to cast a faint shadow on pale ground. Starlight, casting shadows. That used to be the ordinary furniture of the night.

[Close]

It's worth trying to say what darkness is, since we've spent a century acting as if it were nothing — a mere absence, a defect, the universe's way of failing to be lit. But darkness is older than light in our story. We are day creatures who came out of the dark; every one of our ancestors, for four billion years, lived nested in it, and the fire beside which our lineage gathered for the last million years has always been a small island ringed by an enormous, breathing continent. Even cosmically the point holds: all the visible stars, all the galaxies, amount to a rounding error in a universe that is better than 95 percent dark.

Enclosing the commons of the night took about a century, and it was done not out of malice but out of the ordinary human wish to see and be safe. But enclosure can be undone in patches, and unlike most restorations, this one is instant. So: go find it. A desert, a mountainside, a national park, any place the nearest city is a faint dome on the horizon rather than a sky. Go on a moonless night. Wait half an hour while your eyes quietly rebuild their ancient instrument. Then look up. The band of light overhead is the galaxy we live inside, seen edge-on from within — a hundred billion suns behind a hundred billion veils — and it is beautiful, and it was there above every human who ever lived until the last few generations, and it will be there tonight, whether or not anyone is awake to see it.
